subject: latent differences between levels of categorical predictor

messages.author: 5063972801d34964
messages.subject: latent differences between levels of categorical predictor
parts:
I have a model of counts that is potentially simple but has nuances that might benefit from additional latent variable structures. 

 

Assume we have an after-school program in which 100 students compete.  For simplicity, we will say that they succeed or fail in each matchup, and compete in a number of matchups over the course of the program.  The matchups are not head-to-head.  The students are sorted by ability, into classes 1 through 5, with 1 being the lowest and 5 the highest. Students compete only against others in their class, and they participate at different frequencies.  This results in varying numbers of binomial trials per student per class. Many, but not all students participate at multiple levels over the course of the program.

 

What we want to know at any given time is how each student would be expected to perform, on average, if they were forced to compete at the highest level, which is the ultimate goal of the program.

 

I put together the following simulated dataset and basic model:

 

 

### load packages

library(tidyverse)

library(INLA)

 

### reproducibility

 

set.seed(4567)

 

### simulated predictors

 

# trials and success rates by level

 

df <- tibble(trials = round(runif(2e3, min=1, max=250)),

             success = rbinom(2e3, size=trials, prob=.4),

             class=1) %>%

  dplyr::bind_rows(tibble(trials = round(runif(2e3, min=1, max=250)),

                          success = rbinom(2e3, size=trials, prob=.5),

                          class=2)) %>%

  dplyr::bind_rows(tibble(trials = round(runif(2e3, min=1, max=250)),

                          success = rbinom(2e3, size=trials, prob=.6),

                          class=3)) %>%

  dplyr::bind_rows(tibble(trials = round(runif(2e3, min=1, max=250)),

                          success = rbinom(2e3, size=trials, prob=.7),

                          class=4)) %>%

  dplyr::bind_rows(tibble(trials = round(runif(2e3, min=1, max=250)),

                          success = rbinom(2e3, size=trials, prob=.8),

                          class=5))

 

# simulated students with varying abilities

 

student.dat <- tibble(

  ID = seq.int(1:1e2),

  ability = sample(c(-.5, -.25, 0, .25, .5), size=1e2, replace=TRUE))

 

# create the data frame to be modeled

 

df <- df %>%

  dplyr::bind_cols(dplyr::sample_n(student.dat, size=1e4, replace=TRUE))

 

# data frame to predict for each student at the highest level

 

df.preds <- expand.grid(success = NA,

                        class = 1,

                        ID = seq.int(1:100),

                        trials = 1)

 

### the basic model

 

samp.mod <- inla(success ~

                   offset(ability) + # to differentiate simulated students

                   class +

                   f(ID, model="iid"),

                 data=df %>%

                   dplyr::bind_rows(df.preds) %>%

                   dplyr::mutate(class = as.factor(class)),

                 family="binomial", Ntrials=trials,

                 control.predictor = list(link=1)

                 # verbose=TRUE

)

 

### extract and view predictions for success

 

df.preds$pred_success <- round(samp.mod$summary.fitted.values[10001:10100,]$mean,3)

df.preds$pred_success_sd <- round(samp.mod$summary.fitted.values[10001:10100,]$sd,3)

df.preds$success <- NULL

 

head(df.preds, n=20)

 

 

Although this model feels like a good start, there are important aspects of the relationships between levels that this model might not capture, but which I suspect INLA has the additional tools to track. 

 

The first challenge is that, while the simple model captures the *mean* performance at each level of “class,” it doesn’t necessarily reflect the *differences* in difficulties between levels.  For that, we probably want to also track of the performance of students who switch classes.  But limiting the model to those students is undesirable because the students who don’t switch classes also give us useful information about the students not good enough to move up, and because we want to make the best possible predictions on all 100 students, whether they moved up previously or not.

 

It feels like this could employ a “lag” system that indexes differences between students who switch classes.  If so, perhaps this could be an autogression type of specification, maybe using the replicate function, but it could use discrete performances at different classes rather than different time measurements.  But not everyone switches classes, so I am not sure if this is really the best option, and again it is trying to use a “class” series rather than a “time” series. 

 

The second challenge is that it is possible students could  “master” a class of difficulty and over-perform in a way that is not translatable to a higher level. In other words, they may not end up being properly “shrunk” toward the probable ability mean by the simple model because they spend a lot of trials running up the score to an unusual extent at a lower level.  So, for example, the true penalty of moving up one level might only be a few points of success on average, but somebody with a high number of trials and a level-specific amount of success could plummet far more than average when moved up. That’s the sort of thing we want to be aware of before putting a kid in a position to fail.

 

For this second problem, the challenge seems to be also modeling the maximum number of “trials” at each level that are actually useful in predicting success at a different level, although perhaps there is another way to approach it.  I am honestly not sure if there is a simple structure that could model this (perhaps a binned random walk on trials replicated to levels, with trials being an additional predictor in the model?), but am open to ideas. 

 

I’d appreciate any suggestions the list has, especially if they allow this problem to be addressed within a single likelihood.

 

Jonathan
